newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Arafat and Levy at odds on Mideast peace progress.
newsitem.headline: Arafat and Levy at odds on Mideast peace progress.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat fell out diplomatically on Wednesday over whether their meeting had broken the logjam in the Middle East peace process.
Arafat told reporters the meeting on the margins of a European Union foreign ministers' meeting on Tuesday had achieved nothing, while Levy said it had given new impetus to the talks.
Both men spoke after separately meeting with Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke on Wednesday.
"We have every reason to be optimistic. We have taken a step forward," Levy told reporters.
For his part Arafat, who met Derycke earlier, was far from confident that progress had been achieved, and he called on the European Union to use its influence on Israel.

"I am looking to achieve something concrete. We are not asking for the moon," he said. "We are asking the European Union to help get results. It is very important that with their help we can save the peace process."
The peace talks, first launched in Oslo in 1993, have been steadily sliding into crisis since March this year when Israelis began building 6,500 houses in Arab East Jerusalem.
Tuesday's meeting between Arafat and Levy was the first since April.
Former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, assassinated in November 1995, and his successor Shimon Peres both stood by the so-called land for peace accords.
Arafat and Rabin shared the Nobel peace prize in 1994 for their efforts for peace in the Middle East.
But current Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu, to international disapproval, gave the green light for the housing project.
"Mr Rabin, my partner, refused to carry on with the project. So did Peres," Arafat said. "It is very delicate."
However, on Wednesday Levy rejected suspending the building project.
"We had no preconditions yesterday," he said, adding that the Oslo agreement did not specifically rule out building in East Jerusalem.
"Violence must cease. The language must be that of peace," he added.
"We have had many dangers and obstacles to overcome...We now have the most propitious chance to relaunch the peace process," Levy said.
However, Arafat noted on Wednesday Levy had no mandate to discuss the thorny issue of East Jerusalem, and it was unclear what the position of the Israeli government would be.
"We want something more concrete and more interventions from the European Union," he said.
Tuesday's meeting between Arafat and Levy was brokered by the EU.
On Wednesday both men said no timetable had been set for resuming full talks, although Levy said he hoped for progress in the coming days.
